cur:catacombs-lucina-baptism.summary: On a damaged, pale wall two faint red-brown figures can be made out: a larger man reaching out to a smaller, naked figure who stands in water. The scene is commonly identified as John the Baptist baptizing Christ, which would make it one of the very earliest surviving images of the Baptism, though the painting is now very faded.
facts: Commons records this painting in the Crypt of Lucina, the oldest part of the Catacomb of Callixtus.
In early Christian art the baptized Christ is usually shown small and naked, standing in the water, with the Baptist larger beside him – the convention visible here.
cur:catacombs-lucina-baptism.notes: Whether this baptism shows Christ or represents the sacrament of baptism in general is debated; no dove is clearly visible in the surviving paint.

cur:legends-mandylion-genoa.summary: Within a precious frame of gilded silver, the face of Christ appears alone, dark and solemn, its long hair and beard ending in points like the outline of a cloth, surrounded by ten small relief plaques telling the story of King Abgar and the miraculous image of Edessa. Byzantine tradition held the Mandylion to be the cloth on which Christ himself imprinted his face; this image, given by the Emperor John V Palaiologos to the Genoese Leonardo Montaldo in the 14th century, has long been venerated in Genoa as that relic. Scholarly study instead dates the painted image to the Middle Ages and the frame to the 14th century.
facts: Colette Dufour Bozzo's 1969 study found that the image is painted on a cloth pasted onto a wooden board, and dated the outer frame to the late 14th century.

The relic was bequeathed by Leonardo Montaldo, doge of Genoa, to the Basilian monks of San Bartolomeo degli Armeni; it was carried off to France in 1507 and returned a year later, and buried for safety during the siege of 1522.
It is displayed to the faithful in the week following Pentecost.

cur:legends-mandylion-genoa.notes: Dating disputed: it.wikipedia reports earlier studies placing the panel around the year 1000 (textiles, pigments) and C-14 tests giving c. 1240–1280 (62% probability); M. Sturgis (as quoted on shroud.com) gives 1240–90 at 90% probability, from the University of Lecce. The radiocarbon results appear not to be formally published, so the 13th-century date is given as 'reportedly'. Sources disagree on when Montaldo received it (1360s–1380s) and on the date of deposit (1384 or 1388).

cur:manuscripts-kells-arrest-of-christ.summary: Beneath a stylised arch topped by two beasts' heads, Christ stands frontally with arms outstretched, a large, calm figure with curling hair and beard, while two much smaller men seize him by the arms. The arch encloses the words 'Et hymno dicto exierunt in montem Oliveti' — 'when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives'. Christ's open, cross-like pose anticipates the Crucifixion.
facts: The scholar Françoise Henry attributed this page and the Temptation to the artist she called 'the Illustrator'.
Its verso carries a fully decorated text page with Christ's words 'Tunc dicit illis Iesus omnes vos scandalum' (Matthew 26:31).
cur:manuscripts-kells-arrest-of-christ.notes: The Commons file description says '114v' but the miniature is on fol. 114r (Wikipedia; Trinity College).
